tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

Invoke a skill.

When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 15 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.content:
# Memo: provincial ADP execution rates — what the documents can and cannot support

## What an execution rate needs

Two numbers for the same jurisdiction and fiscal year: the original allocation, and the realised
spend. They come from different documents and the second is published later, which is the whole
difficulty.

- Allocation: the development programme table in the jurisdiction's white paper. Punjab
  FY2022-23 is at the White Paper on the Budget 2022-23 - Government of Punjab (p. 74 of the file, printed page 2-21), Table 2.1: Annual Development Programme (Punjab).
- Realised: either the revised estimate column in the *following* year's white paper, or the
  quarterly fiscal operations statement. The federal development line for comparison is at
  the Consolidated Federal and Provincial Fiscal Operations 2022-23 (Q3) (p. 8 of the file, printed page 7), Table 1.3: Development Expenditure.

## Coverage

| Jurisdiction | Allocation series | Realised series | Usable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Punjab | Complete | Complete | Yes |
| Sindh | Complete | Complete | Yes |
| Khyber Pakhtunkhwa | Complete | Two years missing | Mostly |
| Balochistan | Two gaps | Sparse | Marginal |
| Azad Jammu and Kashmir | Sparse | Not published in this form | No |
| Gilgit-Baltistan | Sparse | Not published in this form | No |

The last two rows are the reason the headline number in the draft covers four jurisdictions and not
six. This has to be stated in the note to the table, not buried.

## Traps

1. The revised estimate is itself revised. The figure for a given year in the next year's document
   is not the figure for that year in the document two years later. Record which document the
   number came from, every time.
2. Balochistan's outlay is at the White Paper on the Budget 2022-23 - Government of Balochistan (p. 17 of the file, printed page 1-9), Table 1.1: Balochistan -- Total Budget Outlay and that table
   is on a different footing from the Punjab one — it includes the district development component
   that Punjab reports separately.
3. One jurisdiction reports the programme in Rs million. Converting it is trivial; noticing that it
   needs converting is not, because the column header does not always carry the unit.

# Source selection — BLOCKED

## What this is

A decision record for which publication is used as the reference document for each jurisdiction and
fiscal year, so that two people extracting the same cell get the same number.

## Decided

| Jurisdiction | Reference document family | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Federal | Annual Budget Statement | The only document with the full demand-level detail |
| Punjab | White Paper on the Budget | Consistent layout across the window |
| Sindh | White Paper on the Budget | Same |
| Khyber Pakhtunkhwa | White Paper on the Budget | Same, with the caveat about the split table |

## BLOCKED

Balochistan, Azad Jammu and Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan.

For these three the white paper either is not published every year or does not contain the
budget-at-a-glance table in a comparable form. The candidates are the budget speech, the annual
budget statement, and the citizen budget, and they disagree with one another.

I cannot resolve this without a decision on whether comparability across jurisdictions or coverage
across years matters more. Asked on two occasions, no decision yet. Nothing downstream of this can
be finished, which is why the extraction task list still shows these three as open.

## Not decided, not blocking

Whether the statistical supplements are treated as part of the survey or as separate documents.
Either works for our purposes as long as it is consistent.

# Provincial ADP Execution — Working Folder

This folder holds the work on provincial development spending execution rates.

## Layout

- `01_inputs/` — the extracted budget tables, one CSV per jurisdiction and fiscal year
- `02_scripts/` — the cleaning and reshaping scripts, run them in numerical order
- `03_intermediate/` — the reshaped long-format panel before the execution ratios are computed
- `04_figures/` — the charts for the draft

Run `02_scripts/01_load_inputs.R` first, then `02_reshape_panel.R`, then `03_execution_ratios.R`.
The panel that everything else depends on is written to `03_intermediate/adp_panel_long.csv`.

If the ratios look wrong for Balochistan it is almost always because the revised estimate column
is missing for that year and the script silently falls back to the budget estimate. There is a
check for this at the bottom of `03_execution_ratios.R` but it only warns, it does not stop.

## Known issues

- The AJK figures before FY2015-16 are in a different unit and are not rescaled anywhere yet.
- Two of the KP white papers have the ADP table split across a page break and the second half
  was dropped in the first extraction pass. Both were re-done by hand.

# Memo: what has actually happened to provincial spending since the Eighteenth Amendment

The claim one hears is that devolution shifted a large block of spending to the provinces and that
the provinces have not been able to spend it. Both halves of that are worth checking separately,
because the first is about allocation and the second is about execution, and the documents that
speak to them are different documents.

## The allocation side

The transfer share is the cleanest place to start. The provincial share of the divisible pool is
reported in each jurisdiction's own budget document, and the federal side reports what it
transferred. For Punjab the transfer figure appears in the White Paper on the Budget 2022-23 - Government of Punjab (p. 163 of the file, printed page 4-21), Table 4.1: Share in Federal Divisible Pool (Punjab).
The corresponding federal number for the same year is in the Annual Budget Statement 2021-22 (p. 132 of the file, printed page 3-24), Table 3.3: Total revenue receipts — note
that the federal table is on a gross basis and the provincial table is net of collection charges,
so the two will not agree to the rupee and are not supposed to.

Total provincial outlay across the six jurisdictions has grown faster than nominal GDP over the
window, which is the fact the claim rests on. The Punjab outlay series is at
the White Paper on the Budget 2022-23 - Government of Punjab (p. 29 of the file, printed page 1-21), Table 1.1: Total Budget Outlay (Punjab) and the Sindh series at
the White Paper on the Budget 2019-20 - Government of Sindh (p. 25 of the file, printed page 1-20), Table 1.1: Sindh -- Total Budget Outlay.

## The execution side

Here the documents disagree with each other in a way that matters. The budget documents report
what was allocated. The quarterly fiscal operations statements report what was actually released
and spent. The development programme allocation for Punjab is at
the White Paper on the Budget 2022-23 - Government of Punjab (p. 74 of the file, printed page 2-21), Table 2.1: Annual Development Programme (Punjab); the realised federal development figure for a
comparable period is in the Consolidated Federal and Provincial Fiscal Operations 2022-23 (Q3) (p. 8 of the file, printed page 7), Table 1.3: Development Expenditure. Anyone comparing an
allocation number to a release number without saying which is which will produce an execution rate
that is wrong in a predictable direction.

## Social sector

Education is the head most often quoted. The Punjab current education figure is at
the White Paper on the Budget 2022-23 - Government of Punjab (p. 208 of the file, printed page 5-22), Table 5.1: Education Affairs and Services (Current) and the KP figure at
the White Paper on the Budget 2022-23 - Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (p. 167 of the file, printed page 5-18), Table 5.1: Education Affairs and Services (Current). Both are current expenditure only. Development spending
on education sits inside the development programme line and is not separable from these tables.

## What I want checked before this goes anywhere

1. Whether the outlay series for the two smaller jurisdictions is on the same basis as the four
   larger ones. I suspect it is not.
2. Whether the education figure includes higher education, which moved between departments partway
   through the window in at least two jurisdictions.
3. The rebasing. Any series quoted in levels across the whole window crosses a base-year change and
   the levels shift discontinuously at that point even though the growth rates do not. The break is
   documented and there is no excuse for a chart that ignores it.

# Report on "Provincial Development Spending Execution"

## Summary

The paper documents that provincial development allocations have grown faster than realised
development spending, and interprets the widening gap as evidence of an absorptive-capacity
constraint. The question is a good one and the data assembly is a real contribution. I have two
substantive concerns and a number of smaller ones.

## Substantive

**1. The execution ratio is not measured consistently across jurisdictions.** For two of the six
jurisdictions the realised figure comes from the revised estimate in the following year's budget
document; for the others it comes from the quarterly consolidated statement. These are not the same
object. The revised estimate is an intention as of roughly nine months into the year; the
consolidated statement is a release. The paper needs either a single source for the realised figure
or an explicit demonstration that the two agree where both exist.

**2. The level series crosses a base-year revision.** Table 2 reports outlay in constant prices
across the whole window without acknowledging that the underlying national accounts were rebased
partway through. The growth rates are unaffected but the levels are not, and Table 2 reports levels.
Either splice explicitly and say so, or report growth rates.

## Smaller points

- Two jurisdictions are dropped from the main specification without explanation until the appendix.
  Say it in the text, at the point where the sample is defined.
- The coverage table gives counts but not which years are missing. The pattern of missingness is
  informative here and should be shown.
- The unit of the development programme variable is stated in the text as Rs billion but at least
  one of the source documents reports it in Rs million. Confirm the conversion was applied.
- Footnote 14 cites a page number that does not correspond to the table described.

## Recommendation

Major revision. The core exercise is worth doing and the data work is more careful than most, but
the measurement of the dependent variable has to be put on one footing before the results mean
anything.

## Bottom line

That three-way comparison can't be made from anything currently extracted in this corpus. All three source documents are on disk, but none of the KP 2019-20 figures have been pulled out of them, and the one KP number that *is* available for 2019-20 is not the ADP.

## What each leg of the comparison needs, and what's there

**Federal allocation to KP** — missing. The only federal development series in the corpus is `psdp_federal`, which is the **national PSDP total, with no province split**: 2019-20 = Rs 540,402 mn (Rs 540.4 bn), vintage `psdp_federal::v2`, sourced to `economic_survey_2026`, in `RA Work/tax_effort/clean/psdp_federal_series.csv:11`. There is no province-wise breakdown anywhere in the extracted data. `Sources/Federal/PSDP/2019-20/PSDP 2019-20.pdf` is the document that carries it, unextracted.

**Actual releases** — missing entirely. Per `RA Work/provincial_fiscal_panel/notes/MEMO_fiscal_decentralisation.md:24-30`, releases come from the quarterly Consolidated Fiscal Operations statements, not budget documents. All four quarters for 2019-20 are filed at `Sources/Federal/Fiscal Operations/2019-20/`, and none are extracted — the only fiscal-operations extract in the workspace is `fo_2018_19_q1_extracted.json`, and it came back with `"tables": []`.

**KP's own ADP** — missing for this year. `prov_kp_adp` exists but stops at 2013-14 (`Grants/IGC 2017/submitted/prov_kp_adp_working.csv`, four rows, vintage v0 off `economic_survey_2014`). This is the known gap, not an oversight: `Papers/ADP execution/TASKS.md:9` still has KP white papers open — "two years still failing on the split table" — and the coverage table in `RA Work/adp_execution/notes/MEMO_adp_execution_rates.md` marks KP's realised series as "Two years missing."

## The trap worth naming

The KP series that *does* cover 2019-20 is `prov_kp_outlay` — **Total Budget Outlay**, Rs 332.0 bn (`RA Work/adp_execution/clean/prov_kp_outlay_series.csv:11`). That's the whole provincial budget, current plus development. Substituting it for the ADP would overstate the province's development programme by roughly a factor of three and is exactly the allocation-vs-release / outlay-vs-programme confusion the referee report flags as the reason for major revision (`Papers/Fiscal decentralisation/referee_report.md:12-17`).

Note also that this series is vintage-sensitive: the same cell reads **383.4** in `prov_kp_outlay::v1` (`Conferences/PSDE 2016/prov_kp_outlay_earlier_vintage.csv:11`, ES2022) against **332.0** in v2 (ES2026) — a 13% gap on one number, same year, same series.

## Separate finding, probably a bug

Two files carry `series_id=psdp_federal`, `vintage_label=psdp_federal::v0`, `source_doc=economic_survey_2014` — identical provenance triple — and disagree:

| File | 2010-11 | 2011-12 | 2012-13 | 2013-14 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Downloads/reports/local think tanks/psdp_federal_working.csv` | 341.862 | 377.338 | 389.164 | 445.066 |
| `Papers/Tax effort/data/psdp_federal_series.csv` | 318.0 | 351.0 | 362.0 | 414.0 |

A vintage tag that doesn't uniquely identify a value defeats the purpose of the vintage column, and `TASKS.md:19` says vintage population is "done for the federal side only" — so this is the side assumed clean. Worth resolving before the vintage discussion in section 3 of the draft goes out, since that's the part flagged as referee-bait in `PLAN.md:11`.

## To actually get the answer

Three extractions, in this order: the ADP table from `Sources/Provincial/Khyber Pakhtunkhwa/White Papers/2019-20/` (expect the split-table failure — `RA Work/adp_execution/README.md:22-23` says both affected years were redone by hand), the KP lines from `PSDP 2019-20.pdf`, and the development-expenditure table from the 2019-20 Q4 fiscal operations statement.

One caveat on interpretation when you do have them: 2019-20 is a pandemic year, so a low release-to-allocation ratio will be confounded by the mid-year re-prioritisation, not just absorptive capacity. `PLAN.md:14` already lists dropping the pandemic years as the obvious robustness check.

I should flag that I couldn't extract the PDFs myself — `pdftotext` is present on this machine but not permitted in this session, and the Read tool's PDF path needs `pdftoppm`, which isn't installed. Everything above comes from the CSV/JSON/Markdown layer. If you re-run with PDF extraction allowed, I can pull all three numbers directly.
